messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Juan, a 24-year-old Latin American man, works as a QA Engineer at a tech firm in San Francisco. Despite his steady job and social life, Juan has been increasingly troubled by memories of a devastating explosion that occurred two years ago near the factory where he used to work part-time. The event left several colleagues injured, and the trauma has since shaped much of Juan's experience. On the day of the explosion, Juan had just stepped out for lunch when the building erupted in flames and debris. His coworkers were trapped inside, and although he tried to help, by the time he managed to enter the burning structure, it was too late for some. This memory haunts him, particularly during discussions about workplace safety or any mention of similar accidents on the news. Every time a coworker at his current job starts talking about another industrial accident during a meeting, Juan's heart races and he begins to feel detached from reality, as if he is watching everything from a distance. The feeling intensifies when he reads news stories about disasters or sees them on television, pulling him back into the horror of that day. These triggers have led Juan to engage in counterfactual thinking, where he spends hours imagining different scenarios in which he could have prevented the disaster. Juan's fear of harm is also deeply rooted in his experience. He has come to believe that you can never truly know who might cause such devastation or when it will happen again. This belief exacerbates his negative appraisal that he failed to protect others, leading him to withdraw from discussions about safety measures and avoid any form of media coverage related to similar events. The sense of detachment during trigger moments often leads Juan into a spiral of self-blame and counterfactual thinking. He avoids watching the news or reading about such incidents and has even started skipping work meetings that discuss potential dangers at construction sites, fearing these discussions will bring back painful memories. Juan's avoidance behaviors have begun to affect his job performance. His manager has noticed his absence from critical safety meetings and has expressed concern over Juan’s declining involvement in projects that require close attention to risk assessment. This occupational consequence adds another layer of stress as Juan struggles with the fear that he is letting down his current team, just as he believes he let down his former coworkers. In addition, Juan avoids police interactions, which have become increasingly frequent due to his need for verification and reassurance following every minor incident at work. The fear that authorities might remind him of his failure to protect others has made these encounters particularly distressing. Juan’s belief that nothing good can happen to him anymore is a pervasive thought that colors much of his daily life. This negative outlook has led him to isolate himself socially, as he believes that engaging in normal activities will only lead to more disappointment and pain. What frightens Juan most is the idea that he will continue to relive those moments indefinitely, unable to escape the cycle of fear and regret. It was this escalating sense of helplessness and his deteriorating performance at work that finally pushed Juan to seek therapy. He hopes to find a way to break free from the constant reminders of that day and regain control over his life. His current state is marked by a deep desire for relief from the unrelenting anxiety, coupled with a fear that he might never truly recover from this trauma. Juan’s journey through therapy will likely focus on understanding and addressing these interconnected cycles of triggers, maladaptive strategies, and negative appraisals to help him find a path forward.
